title: Egypt at Carchemish, and a Word for Jacob
summary: The oracles concerning the nations begin with Egypt. A first poem pictures Pharaoh Neco's army marching out in splendor and collapsing at Carchemish on the Euphrates in 605 BC; a second announces that Nebuchadnezzar will come against Egypt itself. The chapter closes with God's promise that Egypt will be inhabited again and with a word of comfort to Israel: though disciplined, Jacob will not be destroyed.
story: At his call, Jeremiah was appointed "a prophet to the nations" (1:5), and chapters 46 to 51 gather his oracles about Judah's neighbors and the great powers. These chapters widen the view: the God who judged Jerusalem also rules Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Babylon, and the rest. Egypt comes first here, which fits the preceding chapters. The remnant had just fled to Egypt for safety (chapters 43 and 44), and this chapter shows that Egypt itself was under God's judgment. The oracle also looks back to the moment that changed the region's balance of power, Babylon's victory at Carchemish, which the book has already tied to the fourth year of Jehoiakim (25:1, 36:1). The promise to Jacob at the end reminds the reader that these oracles serve God's purposes for his own people.
historical:
Carchemish, on the upper Euphrates near today's border between Turkey and Syria, was the site of one of the decisive battles of the ancient world. In 605 BC the Babylonian crown prince Nebuchadnezzar attacked the Egyptian army stationed there under Pharaoh Neco II (who reigned about 610 to 595 BC). The Babylonian Chronicle records the battle, describing an overwhelming Babylonian victory and the pursuit and destruction of the Egyptian survivors near Hamath in Syria. Later that year Nebuchadnezzar's father died, and Nebuchadnezzar returned to Babylon to take the throne. Neco was the pharaoh who had killed King Josiah at Megiddo in 609 BC and then placed Jehoiakim on Judah's throne (2 Kings 23:29-35), so for Judah the defeat of Egypt was more than distant news. British excavations at Carchemish in the early twentieth century found destruction and weapons from this period that many scholars connect with the battle.

The second oracle (verses 13 to 24) announces a Babylonian invasion of Egypt itself. Its date is not given. Some connect it with Nebuchadnezzar's attempt on Egypt in 601 BC, which the Babylonian Chronicle reports ended with heavy losses on both sides; others with the campaign about 568/567 BC mentioned in a later fragmentary Babylonian text (see chapter 43).
cultural:
Egypt's army was known for hiring foreign soldiers, and verse 9 names some of them: Cush (the land south of Egypt along the upper Nile), Put (probably in Libya), and Lud, often understood as Lydia in western Asia Minor, whose soldiers are known to have served Egypt in this period. The image of Egypt rising like the Nile (verses 7 and 8) draws on the river's annual flood, which was the source of Egypt's life and wealth and a symbol of its power. The balm of Gilead (verse 11), a medicinal resin from the region east of the Jordan, was famous in the ancient world; Jeremiah had used the same image for Judah (8:22).

Amon of Thebes (verse 25) was the chief god of the Egyptian state in many periods, worshiped in the vast temples at Thebes (modern Luxor) in Upper Egypt. The beautiful heifer of verse 20 may allude to Egyptian cattle worship, especially the sacred Apis bull of Memphis; the Greek translation of verse 15 reads a question about Apis fleeing, which suggests that early readers heard that allusion. Mount Tabor and Mount Carmel (verse 18) were prominent peaks in northern Israel, images of a conqueror who towers over others.
literary: Verse 1 is a heading for the whole collection of oracles concerning the nations (chapters 46 to 51). In the Greek translation of Jeremiah these oracles stand in the middle of the book, after 25:13, and in a different order; the Hebrew places them near the end. The two poems about Egypt are vivid war poetry, full of short commands ("Harness the horses", "Polish your spears") and sudden reversals. The first poem moves from preparation to rout in the space of three verses, and the voice of God breaks in with a question: "Why am I seeing this?" (verse 5). The phrase "terror is on every side" (verse 5) is a signature expression of Jeremiah (6:25, 20:10). The closing verses 27 and 28 repeat, almost word for word, the promise of 30:10-11, placing Israel's hope beside the nations' judgment.

outline.t: Heading: the word concerning the nations and Egypt at Carchemish
The rout of Egypt's army at the Euphrates
Babylon will come against Egypt itself
Judgment on Egypt's gods and a promise of renewal
Do not be afraid, Jacob My servant

doctrines.note: The battle of Carchemish is described as the Lord's day, "a day of vengeance against His foes" (verse 10). The rise and fall of empires is under God's rule, not only the fortunes of Israel.
God will punish "Amon god of Thebes, along with Pharaoh" (verse 25). The gods and kings Egypt trusted, and those in Judah who trusted in Pharaoh, cannot stand before the God of Israel.
God will discipline Israel justly but not destroy it completely (verse 28). His covenant faithfulness sets Israel's future apart from that of the nations, even as he judges both.

words.note: Neqamah, vengeance or retribution. In the Old Testament, God's vengeance is not personal spite but the restoring of justice against those who have done wrong. Verse 10 calls the battle a day of vengeance, perhaps with Neco's killing of Josiah in view, though the text doesn't say so.

Yasha, to save or deliver, the root of the names Joshua and Jesus. In verse 27 God promises to save Jacob from a distant land. In a chapter about a great power's defeat, the one who truly saves is God.

Mishpat, justice or judgment, here in the phrase "I will discipline you justly" (verse 28). It means the right measure. God's discipline of his people is neither lenient nor destructive; it is fitting and purposeful.

Yaaqov, Jacob, the ancestor of Israel and a name for the whole people. Calling the nation Jacob recalls the patriarch who went down to Egypt and was brought back by God, a pointed reminder in a chapter about Egypt.

christ: The chapter ends with God's promise that he will save his people from a distant place and bring them to rest, and that though he disciplines them he will not make a full end of them. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom God's promises to Israel are kept, and his name comes from the same Hebrew root as the verb to save. The chapter also promises that Egypt will be inhabited again after judgment (verse 26), a small note of hope for a nation outside Israel. Isaiah 19 goes further and pictures Egypt one day worshiping the LORD, and the New Testament sees the gospel going out to all nations. The link here is thematic: the God who judges the nations also intends their healing.

hard.q: Why does the Bible call a bloody battle God's sacrifice and day of vengeance?
hard.a: Verse 10 pictures the slaughter at Carchemish as a sacrifice held by God, an image many readers find disturbing. It uses the language of ancient war poetry, and similar images appear in Isaiah 34:6 and Zephaniah 1:7. The prophets used such language to insist that history's great battles are not random but fall under God's judgment on arrogant powers; Egypt's boast in verse 8, that it would cover the earth and destroy cities, is the pride being judged. Some interpreters stress that this is poetry describing what empires do to each other, interpreted as God's justice, not a celebration of violence. Others emphasize that the Bible does not hesitate to say God judges nations through war, while also longing for a day when war will end (Isaiah 2:4). Readers should neither soften the image nor read it as God's delight in bloodshed, which Ezekiel 33:11 explicitly denies.

questions: Egypt boasted that it would rise like the Nile and cover the earth, then fell in a single battle. What powers in our world seem unstoppable, and what does this chapter suggest about them?
The remnant fled to Egypt for safety, but Egypt itself was under judgment. Where do people look for security that cannot finally provide it?
God tells Jacob not to be afraid, even while promising discipline. How can discipline and comfort come from the same God at the same time?
